extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics), readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and distinctions for judging beauty (taste) and for producing beautiful art: Kantian standards about disinterestedness, universal communicability, genius, and the relation of art to nature and moral feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard subjective private conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging from enlarged thought one must disregard the subjective private conditions of one's own judgement and reflect from a universal standpoint (determinable by placing oneself at the standpoint of others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the maxims for sound judgement: set aside personal, idiosyncratic conditions and test your judgement by imagining the standpoint of others. It helps produce an enlarged, communal judgement rather than a merely private taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect from a universal standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical reflection should proceed from a universal standpoint so that one’s feeling and judgement can be communally assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what would be acceptable not only to yourself but as if it were a rule for everyone. This is contrasted with merely private or particular points of view and forms part of the 'sensus communis' for taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecutive thought (habit of combining maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consecutive thought—the third maxim—requires combining the previous maxims (disregard of private conditions and universal standpoint) into a habit, achieved by constant observance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most difficult maxim: sustained, disciplined practice of the first two leads to judgement that coherently applies across cases (the maxim of Reason).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as sensus communis (faculty of a priori communicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging a priori the communicability of feelings that are bound up with a representation, without mediation of a concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste is described as a communal sense when 'sense' is taken as the reflective feeling of pleasure; a judgement of taste asserts that the pleasure can be communicated universally though not via concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of pure aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste that declares something beautiful must have no interest as its determining ground (it must be disinterested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure aesthetic judgement is not determined by desire, utility, or personal advantage. Interests can be combined later but must not determine the initial judgement of beauty; otherwise it becomes non-pure (e.g., vanity, utilitarian appeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal communicability of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure in a judgement of taste carries the idea that it is universally communicable — the expectation that others should agree with this pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumed universal validity is not a conceptual proof but a feeling that one can and ought to communicate the pleasure to others; Kant links this to duty-like expectation (sensus communis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical (social) interest from pure taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical interest in the Beautiful (e.g., sociability, desire to ornament for society) is separate from pure aesthetical judgement and can confound taste by tying beauty to social advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: adornments, fashions, and social signalling may increase perceived worth, but such empirical interests are not the grounds for a priori judgements of taste. Examples: planting flowers for company versus on a desert island.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual immediate interest in nature signals moral disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: An immediate, intellectual interest in the beauty of Nature (not mere judgement of taste) indicates a frame of mind favorable to the moral feeling and can be a mark of a 'beautiful soul'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to someone who admires a wild flower or bird for its presence, not for vanity or social use; the interest must be immediate and based on the thought that nature produced it (not an artificial copy). If deception (artifice) is revealed the immediate interest disappears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate beauty of Nature from beauty of Art regarding moral interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of Nature can arouse an immediate intellectual interest akin to moral feeling; beauty of Art (or artificial uses of beauty) does not reliably indicate moral goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural beauty's 'presence' pleases without sensible charms or purposes; artificial beauty often ties to vanity or mediated interests and is therefore less indicative of moral disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant arts vs beautiful art (purpose and standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasant arts aim at enjoyment (sensory pleasure) and are judged by sensation; beautiful art aims at reflective pleasure and furthers the culture of mental powers, so its standard is reflective judgement not sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of pleasant arts: entertaining storytelling, arranging a feast, music as 'pleasant noise'. Beautiful art is purposive for itself and concerned with universal communicability of reflective pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful art must seem like nature (purposiveness without apparent design)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product of beautiful art must make us conscious of it as art while yet appear to have purposiveness as if produced by nature (i.e., purposiveness that seems free from arbitrary rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should look natural: the conformity to rules must be punctiliously observed but not painfully apparent. If the form of the schools or rules obtrudes, the product ceases to please as beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness must not look designed (art must not reveal its rulefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although art has a definite design, if that design becomes mere sensation or is achieved only by concepts, the product will not please in the mere act of judging; beautiful art must hide its rule-like production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overt signs that the work was made by following explicit rules or for a definite practical purpose; the work should invite free play of imagination and understanding as if arising naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as rule-giving talent (originality and exemplariness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the innate productive talent through which Nature gives the rule to Art: it produces what cannot be derived from rules, must be original, exemplary (models for others), and cannot be taught as technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties of genius: originality (not producible by rule-learning), produces exemplary works that serve as standards, cannot explain its method, and cannot reliably reproduce at will. Models, not precepts, are the means of passing genius on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius vs imitation/learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is opposed to the spirit of imitation and cannot be acquired by teachableness or learning; great scientific discovery can be taught and followed, but artistic genius furnishes material and form that cannot be fully communicated by rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus someone can learn Newtonian science by steps but cannot be taught to write inspired epic poetry by rules alone. Artistic originality must be supported by mechanical skill (rules, prosody) but not reducible to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art requires a mechanical (rule-governed) element as condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Even beautiful art (product of genius) requires some mechanical element—definite rules and technique—without which the 'spirit' would have no body; execution and form require cultivated talent and schooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant warns against the educational error of removing constraint entirely. Genius supplies raw material/ideas; schools and rules supply form and execution (e.g., prosody in poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate natural vs artificial beauty for judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural beauty is a 'beautiful thing' judgeable without a prior concept of purpose; artificial beauty is a 'beautiful representation' and requires consideration of the concept of what the object is to be (its purpose/perfection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judging natural beauty is a pure aesthetic judgement; judging artificial beauty must account for the perfection of the object relative to its intended purpose (teleological considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits: disgust cannot be made beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one kind of ugliness—disgust—which cannot be represented according to nature without destroying aesthetical satisfaction; disgust prevents aesthetic appreciation and cannot be artfully beautified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While many calamitous or unpleasant things (Furies, war, disease) may be represented as beautiful in art, anything that provokes disgust (an intrusive repulsion) destroys the possibility of aesthetic pleasure and thus artificial beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models not precepts: how genius transmits rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of genius must be abstracted from the product itself: models (exemplary works) are the only means by which the Ideas of genius are transmitted to others, not verbal precepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists' works serve as standards to stimulate like ideas in suitably gifted pupils; imitation in the sense of copying is inadequate—models invite imitation of form and spirit, not mechanical replication.
